dharana.numbering_edition: Jaideva Singh 1979 (dhāraṇā 1 = verse 24; dhāraṇā 82 = verses 105–106 and dhāraṇā 89 = verses 113–114, otherwise one verse each; dhāraṇā 112 = verse 137)
dharana.sanskrit_iast: bhaktyudrekād viraktasya yādṛśī jāyate matiḥ | sā śaktiḥ śāṅkarī nityam bhavayet tāṃ tataḥ śivaḥ ||
dharana.sanskrit_source: GRETIL e-text, compared with Wallis's concordance, Pradīpaka and the Singh scan
sanskrit_variants: verse 121: GRETIL, Pradīpaka and (as far as the OCR shows) Singh read bhavayet; Wallis reads bhāvayet ('one should contemplate'). Kept as printed in GRETIL; the sense 'contemplate' follows the translators.
dharana.rendering: The kind of understanding (mati) that arises from an overflowing of devotion in one who is free of attachment is the power of Śaṅkara (Śiva); let one contemplate it constantly, and then one is Śiva.
dharana.rendering_attribution: School paraphrase drawing on Jaideva Singh (1979), Christopher Wallis and Bettina Bäumer (as printed in Wallis's concordance); not a quotation.
dharana.commentary_note: Singh: mati here is a technical term for pure, dynamic spiritual intuition, full of the auspicious power (śāṅkarī śakti) that can transform life. He gives four steps: a change of values, with detachment from sensuous pleasures; devotion to God; the arising of mati from these; and constant contemplation of it. Devotion, he says, is not just presenting flowers and incense but seeing God in all life and dedicating oneself in word, thought and deed. Singh classes it as śāmbhavopāya. Wallis: 'intense devotion'.
dharana.instruction: Let devotion well up without grasping, and keep returning to the clear understanding it brings.

checked_against: The Mystery Within (2019), Session Two list: 'Dharana 96' = verse 121 (agrees with Singh)

verification.notes: Door index = Singh dhāraṇā number, read directly in Singh's own headings and cross-checked against The Mystery Within's Singh-numbered list and Wallis's concordance. Caveat: Singh was read from an OCR scan, not a print copy in hand.

numbering_variants.mystery_within_parallel: The parallel-translations section of The Mystery Within labels verse 121 'Dharana 98', because from verse 106 on it gives every verse its own number (106 = 83 … 137 = 114). Singh and the same book's Session Two list put this at dhāraṇā 96. Not followed.

seat.label: Any steady, comfortable position (school addition)
seat.summary: Any steady, comfortable position: sitting on a chair, sitting on the floor with support under the hips, or lying on the back. Standing or walking slowly is also acceptable when that is easier. Choose the position in which the body needs the least effort.
seat.honesty: School addition. Verse 121 does not specify a body position. The seat is a convenience so the dharana can be practised; it is not part of the technique and makes no claim of tradition.

geometry.summary: Not a body shape. The map is devotion welling up and, from it, a clear understanding that is itself the power of the sacred.
geometry.svg_hint: a spring welling up into a clear pool, with light reflected on its surface
geometry.honesty: Geometry records the dharana's own map of attention, not a body shape. Locations marked 'commentarial' come from commentary, not from the verse.

reaction.name: Devotion becomes understanding
reaction.summary: School metaphor only: devotion that wells up without grasping turns into a clear understanding, which is then cherished constantly. Not a biochemical or medical claim.

breath.lands_in: wherever the breath naturally ends; this door places nothing on the breath
breath.cue: Natural breath. Count about four in and four out only if it helps you settle, then let the count go. No forced hold.
breath.honesty: The counts are an optional school pacing aid, not part of the verse. Hold is always 0: this school never adds a deliberate breath-hold.

orientation.cue: Let devotion well up, and stay with the understanding it brings
orientation.gravity: Let the floor or chair carry the body completely; there is no posture to hold
orientation.degrees_hint: No angle target: the VBT gives no posture for this dharana

attention.secondary: The quiet understanding that arises from it, contemplated again and again

adiyogi.verse_paraphrase: The kind of understanding (mati) that arises from an overflowing of devotion in one who is free of attachment is the power of Śaṅkara (Śiva); let one contemplate it constantly, and then one is Śiva.
adiyogi.method_summary: Turn toward whatever you hold sacred (the divine, life itself, a teacher or an ideal) and let devotion well up, without wanting anything from it. Notice the quiet, clear understanding that arises. Contemplate that understanding, and return to it often through the day.

honesty.disclosure: Door 096 follows Vijñāna Bhairava Tantra dharana 96 (verse 121) in Jaideva Singh's numbering. The door-to-dharana index is a School of 112 Doorways teaching device. Singh's sequence is one edition's count, not an ancient one-to-one canon. The seat, counts, reaction and beat scripts are school additions.
honesty.notes: pairing_type is school_device: the dharana is the content, while the door index, seat and pacing are the school's.
flags: Door index = Jaideva Singh dharana number: Door 096 is dharana 96, verse 121. Other editions number differently (see dharana.numbering_variants).
The seat, breath counts, reaction metaphor, attention-map drawing and beat scripts are school devices, not part of the verse.
The English is a school paraphrase, not a quotation from any translator.
No medical claims. Reaction names are metaphors, not biochemistry.

safety.pain_rule: Pain is information. Pause, regress, or exit. Never push through sharp pain.
safety.open_seat_alternate: This door needs no particular posture: sit on a chair, sit on the floor with support, or lie down. Eyes may stay open.
safety.contraindication_notes: General practice caution only; not medical advice. Devotion here is inner and freely given; it never requires giving up your judgement, your boundaries or your relationships. If anything feels distressing (dizziness, agitation, strong emotion), stop, open the eyes and rest attention on the feet and the floor.
